item.title: First Thing: Court files show how federal agents spied on anti-ICE protesters | Martin Belam
item.description:
Undercover agents infiltrated meetings, private chats and local events. Plus Wile E Coyote returns to the big screen

Good morning. The extent to which federal law enforcement targeted political opponents and peaceful organizers has been laid bare in newly disclosed court documents.

Internal investigative files reveal that the Department of Homeland Security launched a sweeping surveillance operation against anti-ICE protesters, major labor unions and left-leaning advocacy groups – sending undercover agents to infiltrate community meetings and issuing administrative subpoenas to seize financial records. The documents show that DHS investigators obtained financial records of unions and non-profits, as part of an inquiry into “domestic terrorist financing”.

What did undercover government agents do? They infiltrated community meetings, joined private activist Signal chats and surreptitiously recorded audio at local events – including a “resistance skills training” at a public library and a sparring session at a church gym, where an agent accidentally dropped his recording device. Agents posed as activists and actively engaged participants by offering to help with “direct-action” protests.

How have activists responded? Emilia González Avalos, the executive director of Unidos MN, a Minneapolis social justice non-profit group, said: “I believe that this is a clear attempt to intimidate us, to punish and politically repress disagreement and difference. And that is not the America that we have built through hundreds of years. And it’s definitely not the America that we are organizing for.”

Where did the attack take place? The attack took place in Sevastopol, the biggest city in Russian-annexed Crimea. ​The regional governor, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said a woman had been arrested on suspicion of ⁠assassinating Shageyev on behalf of Ukrainian special services.

What has Poland said about Russian activity there? A Russian plan to kill a Ukrainian American citizen in Warsaw was thwarted by Poland before it could be carried out, the Polish prime minister has said. Donald Tusk said it was the first time that “someone on the order of Russia” had sought to attack a US citizen on the territory of another Nato country.

item.title: Patriot missiles have been a godsend for Ukraine against Putin, but they’re running out. Kyiv needs help and fast | Jack Watling
item.description:
Europe and Nato have known for years that interceptor production can’t keep up with demand and now disaster looms, putting us all in danger

“Invincible.” That was how Vladimir Putin described Russia’s latest generation of ballistic missiles in 2018. In 2022 he would unleash this arsenal to strike across Ukraine, hitting command centres, critical infrastructure and airfields. Then, in 2023, Ukraine received Patriot air defence systems from its international partners. The US-supplied missile interceptor would prove to be an effective shield against Russian strikes.

But this year, supplies of Patriot missiles have run out and Kyiv has suffered the consequences. Intercepts have gone from more than 70% to none, so that night after night Russia strikes Ukraine’s infrastructure with impunity. This tragedy was long foretold, and there are no quick fixes.

item.title: No substitute: Kuwaits future tied to Hormuz strait fate
Senator Van Hollen: Iran war is 'exhibit A' of limits of US power
item.description:
Today, there is no all-out war, no peace, and no light at the end of the Strait of Hormuz. The Trump administration’s crack at transforming Iran is drifting along in the Persian Gulf, as on-again, off-again negotiations fail to resolve a conflict that has roiled the global economy while the president’s approval ratings plunge.

Meanwhile, the Gaza Peace Plan is sinking, too, leaving ordinary Palestinians in a state of abject misery amid the rubble and tent cities of Gaza, cowering from Israeli air strikes that have killed more than 1,200 people since a “ceasefire” went into effect in Oct. 2025.

To assess whether there’s a way out of these dismal situations, Responsible Statecraft spoke to Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), a potential 2028 presidential candidate who is known for being one of the Senate’s most vocal critics of Israeli conduct and of AIPAC’s influence on the Congress.

This is a partial transcript of Van Hollen’s podcast interview with Martin Di Caro, edited for length and clarity. You can listen to the full conversation on the History As It Happens podcast here.

Martin Di Caro: Let's begin with the Iran war. In June, the House and Senate passed a concurrent War Powers resolution. It directed the president to remove U.S. forces from hostilities. The administration says it does not have to abide by the vote because of the ceasefire, which it says reset the 60-day withdrawal clock.

Is the War Powers Act of 1973 irreparably broken?

Sen. Van Hollen: Well, it's very damaged. Donald Trump has really shredded its provisions and done so with the complicity of Senate Republicans. Our constitutional framers believed that, by setting up a separate branch of government with its own powers, including the power to declare war, that as an institution Congress would protect its prerogatives. But now we have a Republican Party that is just a rubber stamp for Donald Trump… It's my strong view that this was an illegal war when Donald Trump started it and it is an illegal war now as he continues it in violation of the concurrent War Powers resolution.

Di Caro: What other means does Congress have at its disposal to stop an unnecessary war?

Van Hollen: Ultimately, Congress has to use its power of the purse. I've been very clear: not one penny for this illegal war. As you know, the administration has asked for a supplemental of around $70 billion. My view is Congress should not appropriate those funds because by doing so, we'd be giving consent and approval to an illegal war retroactively. So it's very important that we hold the line and not provide that funding. We're also expending munitions at a tremendous and expensive rate. That's another constraint potentially on the administration's continuation of the war, at least at the [prior] intensity level.

Di Caro: One more question about the War Powers Act and Congress's failure going back decades to restrain the executive. For example, the Libya intervention under Barack Obama in 2011. The United Nations did authorize NATO intervention there to protect civilians, but when Congress challenged President Obama about the 60-day withdrawal clock — this was in June 2011 — Harold Koh, a legal adviser at the State Department, testified on Capitol Hill.

He said, “As everyone recognizes, the legal trigger for the automatic pullout clock — hostilities — is an ambiguous term of art that is defined nowhere in the statute. The legislative history which we cite makes clear there is no agreed upon view of exactly what the term hostilities would encompass. Nor has that standard ever been defined by any court or by Congress itself.”

I have a two-part question. What do you make of that statement 15 years on? And do you regret voting in support of the Obama intervention in Libya?

Van Hollen: No, to [answer your] second point, and here's why. I recognize this is a very gray area in certain instances. And the Libya circumstances were a gray area. Iran is not a gray area. Not one bit. We've obviously lost 18 service members. There's no question about whether or not we're engaged in hostilities in Iran.

In the case of Libya, as you know, in addition to the U.N. resolution and NATO's involvement, the Arab League also urged the United States to support the effort as part of a coalition to prevent what was viewed as an imminent massacre of hundreds of thousands of people. And it was exclusively air power. So I do recognize that it was a murky area, but my view was that for the limited period that the Obama administration was engaged in that action, with the support of both the U.N. and the Arab League, the administration's argument was sound. At least it wasn't frivolous. Let's put it that way. Whereas in the case of the Iran situation, the Trump administration's argument is plainly frivolous.

Di Caro: In Libya, it started with good intentions, but there was mission creep and it ended up a regime change operation after President Obama had said he would not [seek that outcome] militarily. And ultimately Libya became a failed state. Maybe it would have been a failed state without U.S. intervention, but I think Libya is an important example in this long story of how we got here today.

Van Hollen: I agree that it resulted in mission creep. No doubt about it. You asked me about the original justification, but if you're looking at the results, on the one hand, it was successful at preventing a mass slaughter, and I think that's obviously a good thing. On the other hand, as you say, the mission did seem to evolve and resulted in the toppling of Gaddafi, and Libya became a failed state. So, I'm not suggesting the Libya operation was an ultimate success. I do think it was a limited success with respect to its original purpose.

Di Caro: Let's move on to Israel now. You wrote an op-ed in the New York Times calling on Democrats to reckon with their failure to use U.S. leverage to restrain Israel's conduct. Some former members of the Biden administration have recently come under intense public scrutiny for not conditioning aid to Israel as it was destroying Gaza. Yet today, U.S. weapons and U.S. manufactured bulldozers keep flowing to Israel. Why is that?

Van Hollen: It's because we still haven't mustered enough votes to stop it. We've made gains. I remember in the March-April period of 2025 when there was a full blockade of all food and humanitarian assistance into Gaza that lasted almost 80 days. We had about 17 votes or thereabouts in the Senate to prevent the transfer of U.S. weapons to the Israeli government. In a more recent vote, we were able to secure 40 Democratic senators to block weapons and bulldozers. So, the trend is in the right direction, at least on the Democratic side. Now, on the Republican side, you have a continued blank check to the Netanyahu government regardless of the conduct of Israel, whether in Gaza or the West Bank.

So I guess the answer to your question is there's growing sentiment that United States taxpayers should stop providing a blank check to Israel. My view is that any offensive weapons should also be conditioned on withdrawal of the Israeli occupation in the West Bank, according to an agreed upon timetable.

Di Caro: You've been one of the more vocal senators criticizing Israel. I often wonder if privately your colleagues in the Senate voice those same opinions, but they're afraid to say them publicly.

Van Hollen: The short answer is yes, that is very true. Mine was a lonely position a number of years ago. In fact, before the war in Gaza, I was very focused on trying to end the Israeli occupation of the West Bank and to use [U.S.] leverage to do so. I had colleagues even then who agreed with me privately, but it was politically inconvenient for them to agree openly.

And then with the war in Gaza, people have witnessed the horrendous destruction, what human rights organizations, historian Omer Bartov, and others have concluded is genocide. They have the right analysis. So, more and more of [my] colleagues are finally waking up to the idea that providing a blank check to the Netanyahu government is undermining our security in the region and undermining our position around the world.

Di Caro: It's not unusual for Congress to trail public opinion. That was the case during the Vietnam War. The public turned against the war before a majority in Congress did. But across the political spectrum now, especially among younger voters — left, center, and right — they have soured on U.S. support for Israel. Why are some of your Senate colleagues still afraid to vote against Israel? Is it as simple as AIPAC or is there more to it?

Van Hollen: The number one driver is politics here in the United States. It’s AIPAC. AIPAC has traditionally been a very strong political player. They weigh into elections. Look, we've just witnessed them putting $30 million into the race against Abdul El-Sayed [in the Michigan Senate race]. They’re involved in many other races. They've shown a willingness to use their political muscle to defeat any candidate that doesn't support unconditional aid to Israel. Now, their position is obviously weakening among Democrats. And there are a lot of other groups in this space, including other prominent Jewish political organizations like J Street, that take a very different position. But AIPAC has been the biggest player, and that is why Congress remains largely in a bubble on this issue, although the bubble is being pierced here and there.

Di Caro: Is U.S. hegemony waning and is that such a bad thing for the rest of the world?

Van Hollen: I would say two things are happening. One is that complete U.S. dominance is certainly waning. We've seen the ongoing rise of other powers, China being the biggest one.

Di Caro: Primacy. You're referring to primacy?

Van Hollen: Yes, I'm talking about the U.S. being an unchallenged leader. What it means, though, is other countries do need to take on more responsibility for their collective defense. I will say that the Trump administration has completely shredded and destroyed U.S. credibility. We used to be a champion for international law and the rules-based order — I would say a very imperfect one. I'm well aware of that, and the Biden administration did a lot of damage in that regard, with respect to not applying international law in the case of Gaza, for example. The Trump administration has just abandoned [international law] altogether. It’s in the United States interests to again work to adhere to a rules-based order internationally. There's a lot of repair work to be done there.

Di Caro: To me, this often comes down to the ability to recognize the limits of power... To those of us who’ve been arguing for a more restrained U.S. foreign policy, the primacists don't understand the limits of power — even though we're seeing it everywhere today, and not just with the United States.

Van Hollen: Well, I think you're right. I think your analysis is spot on. What we're witnessing in Iran is Exhibit A of the limits of power. Donald Trump thought he could go into Venezuela, grab Maduro, and in a short period of time he can do whatever he wants anywhere in the world. Obviously that's just not true. So we need to reassess the huge military footprint we have around the world.

item.title: Gas supply rises as Summit fully, Excelerate partially resumes operations
item.description:
Some relief may come today, Saturday, after 25 consecutive days of severe gas shortages. The Summit LNG terminal is now operating at full capacity, while Excelerate Energy’s terminal has partially resumed operations. As a result, gas supply has increased since early Saturday. However, it may take several more days for the gas crisis to ease completely.

Petrobangla oversees LNG imports with the approval of the Energy Division, while its subsidiary, Rupantarita Prakritik Gas Company Limited (RPGCL), handles the imports. Two officials involved in LNG supply told Prothom Alo that gas supply from Summit’s terminal began at 4:00am today at 460 million cubic feet (mmcf) and from Excelerate’s terminal at 300 mmcf.

Petrobangla Chairman Md Abdul Mannan told Prothom Alo that gas is now being supplied from both terminals. Summit’s terminal is operating at full capacity, while Excelerate’s terminal is supplying gas partially. The increased supply will provide some relief to consumers, he said.

There are two floating LNG terminals in Maheshkhali, Cox’s Bazar, for supplying imported LNG. US company Excelerate Energy’s terminal has a capacity of 600 mmcf, while local company Summit’s terminal has a capacity of 500 mmcf.

Excelerate’s terminal was shut down after a fire incident on 21 July. This reduced gas supply and worsened the crisis. From household cooking stoves to industrial plants and power generation, operations were disrupted. The reduction in power supply increased load-shedding. Long queues also formed at filling stations as CNG-powered auto-rickshaws and other vehicles struggled to obtain fuel.

item.title: At least 38 dead after Indonesia's magnitude-7.7 earthquake
item.description:
INDONESIA-QUAKE/

At least 38 people died after an earthquake of magnitude 7.7 and dozens of aftershocks struck off eastern Indonesia on Saturday, officials said, as rescue workers rushed to reach areas closest to the epicentre.

Tsunami waves of less than 1 metre (3 feet) were recorded in several areas of the Southeast Asian nation after the early morning tremor. The tsunami warning was lifted about three hours after the quake.

"As of 15:00 (0800 GMT), the recorded figures are 38 fatalities, two people seriously injured, 11 with minor injuries," Suharyanto, head of the National Disaster Management Agency, or BNPB, told a televised press conference. He added that approximately 2,000 people had fled to safer ground.

Earlier, rescuers in the port town of Maumere found 20 dead, six injured and two trapped under the rubble, said Fathur Rahman, head of the city's rescue agency. Maumere is the main town in Sikka Regency on Flores Island in the east of Indonesia's vast archipelago.

Suharyanto said residents remain trapped in several buildings in earthquake-affected areas and there are reports of landslides blocking several roads.

Teams have yet to reach Nagekeo, the region closest to the epicentre, and communications signals there had been affected, Fathur told Reuters. Attempts to reach Nagekeo by car were blocked by landslides, while another team was attempting to go by ferry, he said.

About 2,000 residents in Nagekeo evacuated, and damage was reported to a number of houses, warehouses and government facilities, the BNPB said. Authorities also reported traffic congestion and power outages affecting parts of the regency, it said.

The governor of East Nusa Tenggara Province, Emanuel Melkiades Laka Lena, told a press conference at least five people died from collapsing rubble as they slept.

Parts of a building collapsed into dust and rubble as people screamed and ran in the street, a video on Facebook, verified by Reuters as being at a port in Maumere, showed.

"The quake was massive, the shock was so strong, we were resting at home with family," said Nona, a 51-year-old resident of Talibura, a village in East Nusa Tenggara. "There were 13 of us inside the house and we all ran to save ourselves."

Strong shaking was felt across East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara and parts of South Sulawesi, and residents in several areas reported shaking lasting about one minute, the BNPB said in a statement.

"Most of the people felt the shock and scattered out of their homes," it said.

A hospital in the district of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara Province was moving patients outside, Kompas TV footage showed, and Kompas.com reported at least one landslide.

Indonesian geophysics agency BMKG recorded the first quake at 4.58 a.m. (2158 GMT) at a depth of 15 km (9 miles), followed by several aftershocks.

In 1992 the same area was hit by a magnitude-7.5 quake, causing extensive destruction at that time, the agency said.

Australia's tsunami warning centre said the undersea earthquake would pose "no tsunami threat to the Australian mainland, islands or territories".

Indonesia straddles the "Pacific Ring of Fire", a seismically active zone, where different plates on the earth’s crust meet, creating a large number of earthquakes and volcanoes.

item.title: Yemeni official says Houthi attack kills 8, rebels claim Saudi strike
item.description:
A military official from Yemen’s internationally recognized government said a Houthi strike Friday on the port city of Mokha killed eight people, while the Iran-backed rebels said they had also attacked a Saudi oil installation.
A years-long truce in Yemen’s civil war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed authorities appeared to collapse last month, with the rebels carrying out deadly attacks on government-held areas.
The rebels have also declared a maritime blockade on Saudi ports, attacking ships in the Red Sea and claiming strikes on oil infrastructure.
The Houthis “fired five missiles at commercial ships unloading at the port, and two ships are on fire,” the Yemeni official said of the attack on Mokha, which was also hit earlier this week.
Two security personnel were among the eight killed, the official said.
Houthi media, meanwhile, quoted a rebel military source as saying the group had attacked a Saudi Aramco site in Najran, in southwest Saudi Arabia, “by means of a drone, and the operation achieved its objective.”
The group had said it carried out an attack on an Aramco facility in Jizan the day before.

item.title: Measles deaths cross 900 amid vaccination coverage concerns
item.description:
The number of children who have died from measles and measles-like symptoms in Bangladesh has crossed 900, with eight more deaths reported in the 24 hours to yesterday morning.
A total of 902 children have died from measles or symptoms of the disease since March 15, according to the latest data from the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Of the deaths, 803 were among children with measles-like symptoms, while 99 were confirmed measles cases.
The DGHS disclosed the figures in its latest measles situation report yesterday afternoon.
No death among confirmed measles patients was reported in the last 24 hours. During the period, 70 new confirmed cases were detected, while 728 children developed measles-like symptoms.
Another 700 children were admitted to hospitals, while 549 were discharged after treatment.
Between March 15 and Saturday, Bangladesh recorded 141,776 suspected measles cases and 17,800 confirmed cases. A total of 123,494 patients were hospitalized, of whom 119,089 have since been discharged.
The continued deaths despite an ongoing vaccination campaign have raised questions about the government’s measures to contain the outbreak.
Public health experts say many children in the target age group remain outside vaccination coverage. The absence of adequate guidelines and coordinated instructions has also complicated the situation.
They believe the outbreak could have been brought under control sooner had appropriate decisions been taken at the initial stage and effectively implemented at the grassroots level.
Experts also said it is important to determine whether vaccinated children have developed sufficient antibodies to protect them against measles.
However, DGHS Director General Prabhat Chandra Biswas said infections have declined somewhat and are expected to fall further.
He said awareness campaigns are being conducted alongside vaccination drives.
The DGHS has also launched an initiative to determine the actual causes of death among children who died after developing measles. Divisional directors have been instructed to review whether the deaths were caused by measles or pneumonia.
Biswas said pneumonia deaths following the measles outbreak have not emerged as a significant separate issue, although pneumonia naturally causes many child deaths in Bangladesh.
Former IEDCR director Professor Mahmudur Rahman said controlling infections is essential to reducing deaths and that ensuring proper vaccination coverage should be the first priority.
Public health and vaccine expert Tajul Islam A Bari also questioned the government’s vaccination coverage figures, saying they do not reflect the actual situation.
He said the vaccination programme’s target was around 18 million in 2010. Despite the population increase since then, a similar target has been set for measles-rubella vaccination, which he said is inappropriate.
A Bari said measles cannot be controlled without vaccinating children who have been left out of the programme. At least 95% of a population must be vaccinated to effectively control transmission, he said.
EPI Deputy Director Sabbir Ahmed said the Expanded Programme on Immunization is conducting initiatives to vaccinate children aged six to 59 months who have not yet received vaccines.
Health workers have been instructed to go door to door to identify unvaccinated children and administer vaccines, he said.
Sabbir said children below six months and those above five years are currently being affected by measles at higher rates, meaning children outside the routine vaccination age are also at risk.
He expressed hope that improved vaccination coverage would reduce both infections and deaths.
Asked whether children outside the specified age range would be included in the vaccination program, he said there was no such plan for now.
Public health expert Mushtaq Hossain said weaknesses in the healthcare system, alongside vaccination gaps, are contributing to child deaths.
Some deaths could have been prevented if the healthcare system had been more effective, he said, adding that public awareness also remains inadequate.
Mushtaq advised parents to keep children with fever separated from others and seek treatment at a local health centre if the fever persists.
He called for stronger primary healthcare facilities, particularly centres providing care between intensive care units and home-based treatment. Such facilities could help save critically ill patients while reducing pressure on major hospitals, he said.
Professor Benazir Ahmed, former chief scientific officer of the IEDCR, said the government had not taken sufficient action to tackle the outbreak.
He pointed to the health minister’s announcement that another 100,000 children would be brought under vaccination coverage, saying this indicates coverage remains below the desired level.
At least 95% of children in the target age group must be vaccinated, he said. Otherwise, transmission will continue among unvaccinated children.
Benazir acknowledged that identifying unvaccinated children is difficult but said it is possible with adequate funding and planned initiatives. He recommended village- and neighbourhood-based campaigns to raise awareness among parents.
Professor Mahmudur Rahman, former IEDCR director and chairperson of the National Verification Committee on measles-rubella vaccination, called for coordinated decision-making involving multiple experts.
He said children below six months are also being infected, requiring a separate strategy.
Given the continued transmission, authorities should also consider vaccinating children outside the routine age range, he said.
Rahman said several technical issues also need to be addressed to bring the outbreak under control. Sustainable improvement will not be possible unless those issues are identified and addressed based on expert recommendations, he added.

item.title: Gas crisis brings daily life to a standstill
item.description:
The gas crisis in Dhaka has shown no sign of easing, with severe shortages disrupting both transportation and household activities across the capital since Saturday morning.
CNG stations are struggling with low gas pressure, forcing drivers of CNG-run vehicles to spend hours in queues. Even after waiting for several hours, many receive enough gas for only one or two trips.
The crisis has also hit households, with gas stoves remaining unusable for hours in many areas. Families are being forced to rely on LPG cylinders, electric stoves and restaurant food for cooking.
The situation has created widespread hardship in Dhaka and other parts of the country, with industrial production and businesses also facing disruptions.
A visit to several areas of the capital and conversations with affected people revealed the extent of the crisis.
Long queues of vehicles were seen at CNG stations in Gabtoli, Kallyanpur, Kalshi, Kazipara and Shewrapara.
Private cars, microbuses and auto-rickshaws were forced to wait for extended periods because of reduced gas supplies.
Khalil, a private car driver waiting at Mohona Filling Station in Gabtoli, said the gas crisis had worsened.
“Gas may be available in small quantities late at night, but there is hardly any during the day,” he said.
After waiting in line for around one and a half hours, he received enough gas for only two trips.
“Now I am standing in line again. There is no one to see our suffering,” he said.
The situation was similar in Demra, where transport workers were waiting more than four hours at some CNG filling stations for gas.
Long queues of vehicles stretched in front of stations, while drivers said they were struggling to earn enough because they could not make enough trips.
Filling station owners were also reporting losses as gas sales declined.
Md Bashir Howlader, a rent-a-car driver at Russell Filling and CNG Station, said he was losing money every day because of the shortage.
“I cannot take long-distance passengers. We cannot leave passengers in the vehicle and go for gas anymore because we have to stay in line for three to five hours,” he said.
“If this continues, our families will have to go hungry.”
The gas shortage was particularly severe in Mugda, Maniknagar, Sabujbagh, Khilgaon, Banasree and Hajipara, where gas pressure was reportedly extremely low.
Several filling stations were seen displaying signs saying gas was unavailable.
Kabi Hossain, a driver waiting at Shanto Filling Station, said he had been in the queue since 9am but had still not received gas by 2pm.
“The crisis is becoming more severe every day. Even if I do not get gas, I have to pay the owner Tk1,200 every day. I do not know what to do in this situation,” he said.
The gas crisis was also severe in Uttara, where supplies had stopped at many CNG filling stations.
Stations that remained operational were seeing long queues because of low pressure.
Kamal Ahmed, manager of Khandakar Filling Station, said a large portion of the transport sector depended on gas.
“Because of the low pressure, long queues of vehicles are forming. There is nothing we can do to solve the problem,” he said.
CNG driver Jasim said he had been waiting since the previous night but had still not received gas.
“If this continues, how will I run my family? How will I pay my children’s school fees? I cannot take this much mental pressure anymore,” he said.
The gas crisis has also severely disrupted household activities in different parts of Dhaka.
In many areas, gas stoves remain unusable for hours, forcing families to cook with LPG cylinders or electric stoves. Some households have also turned to restaurants for their daily meals.
The crisis is meanwhile threatening industrial production and disrupting business activities across the country.
Jahanara Begum, a resident of Sector 6 in Uttara, said gas was usually available early in the morning, allowing families to prepare food for the entire day.
“But for the past three days, there has been almost no gas. We have been forced to buy food from restaurants,” she said.
Schoolteacher Amena Begum said cooking for children at her school’s daycare had also stopped because of the shortage.
“We have to buy food from restaurants and provide it to the children. LPG is also not easily available. The prices of induction stoves and rice cookers have also gone up,” she said.

item.title: 1.36 million Class 11 seats vacant, higher education at risk
item.description:
Of nearly 2.5 million seats available for Class 11 admission nationwide, around 1.36 million are expected to remain vacant this year after the pass rate in the SSC and equivalent examinations fell.
Education experts say the decline in student numbers could affect higher education over the next 2-3 years, with private universities likely to face the greatest pressure.
A total of 1.14 million students passed the 2026 SSC and equivalent examinations, against around 2.5 million Class 11 seats in colleges and madrasas. Even if every successful student enrolls, around 1.36 million seats will remain vacant.
Vacant seats, however, do not mean an equal number of students will disappear from the higher education pipeline. Some may pursue technical or other education, study abroad or discontinue their studies after secondary education.
A large portion of students entering Class 11 in 2026 will sit for HSC examinations in 2028 before seeking admission to universities and other higher education institutions.
The impact of this year's lower SSC pass numbers could therefore become most visible in the 2028-29 academic year, particularly at less-demanded private universities, less popular subjects and some institutions outside major cities.
Leading public universities, medical colleges and engineering institutions are unlikely to face similar pressure because demand for their limited seats remains high.
Education stakeholders say the bigger question is whether Bangladesh will have enough students to fill existing higher education capacity in the future.
The large number of vacant Class 11 seats could leave a significant portion of institutional capacity unused, making it necessary to reassess existing institutions, education quality and subject-wise demand rather than creating more institutions, departments or seats.
Experts, however, caution against declaring a long-term student shortage based on one year's SSC results. Trends in SSC and HSC examinees and passers over the next few years will be crucial.
If the decline continues, universities and colleges could face more vacant seats, while questions could arise over the use of teachers, infrastructure and funding. Private institutions may have to compete harder to attract students.
Some experts also see the decline as an opportunity to improve teacher-student ratios, expand research and strengthen skills-based education.
University Grants Commission member Professor Dr Abdullah-Al-Mamun told Dhaka Tribune that the 2026 results were based on genuine and proper evaluation, which could contribute to qualitative changes in the education system.
He said previous systems had encouraged schools, colleges and teachers to inflate results, including through pressure to push pass rates as high as 96%. He also alleged that schools, colleges and madrasas were established without proper planning under a system of infrastructure development and institutional expansion that facilitated corruption and looting.
"Schools and colleges were approved without any proper calculation or assessment," he said, linking this lack of planning to the emerging shortage of students.
According to Professor Abdullah-Al-Mamun, establishing institutions and infrastructure served 3 purposes: creating opportunities for corruption, empowering local musclemen through managing committees or governing bodies, and creating a network of vested interests to protect the system.
Asked about the future impact on higher education, he said public universities would not be significantly affected, but weaker private universities could face a crisis.
He also questioned the need for so many universities.
"Universities were established at will to create an opportunistic class. It was a popular programme," he said, alleging that private universities were approved without adequate quality control and often based on political ambitions.
"Now, when the government is moving towards quality, these universities may face a kind of student crisis. But I do not think they will face a very severe crisis. Was there really a need for 116 private universities?"
Educationist Rasheda K Chowdhury said the vacant seats reflected a mismatch between educational capacity and actual demand.
"What will happen with so many vacant seats? Clothes have to be cut according to the size of the body. We are cutting more than the size," she said.
She said too many schools, colleges and madrasas had been established without considering demand and suggested encouraging students who fail to pursue technical education.
"There will be admission battles at Dhaka College, Notre Dame and all good colleges. Weak colleges will face a shortage of students," she said.
Chowdhury said the decline would eventually reach higher education but public universities were unlikely to face a student shortage because demand remained high. Based on recent trends, she said, only around 3% of GPA-5 holders were admitted to Dhaka University.
"There will be no vacant seats there. But private universities may face problems," she said.
She recommended a census of educational institutions at both the secondary and higher secondary levels based on actual demand, saying many institutions had been established indiscriminately, sometimes at the request of MPs.
Dhaka Education Board Secretary Professor SM Kamal Uddin Haider said there was no need to approve so many schools and colleges, noting that around half of the seats were also vacant last year.
"A policy decision is certainly needed on this issue," he said, adding that weak colleges would face a student crisis.
He said some HSC graduates who fail to secure public university places may also lack the financial means to attend private universities, potentially creating a crisis there.
However, he said the impact on private universities may be limited because their semester-based admission system allows students to enrol for around 6 months.
Professor Haider called for a survey to determine where institutions have sufficient demand.
"In the past, so many institutions were given recognition, one right next to another. There was no proper assessment of where they would find students," he said.
If the student shortage becomes severe, he suggested merging multiple private institutions while protecting teachers' and employees' jobs.
"Banks can be merged in the country, so what is the problem with educational institutions?" he asked.

item.title: Rampant Bangladesh make history with first-ever Test win in Australia
item.description:
A dominant Bangladesh stunned hosts Australia to win the first Test by nine wickets in Darwin on Sunday for a historic maiden Test victory on Australian soil.

After bowling Australia out for 284 and needing 57 to win, the visitors cruised past the total when Mominul Haque slashed Beau Webster to the backward point boundary.

Bangladesh dominated Australia throughout the match and the margin of victory will send shockwaves through the cricketing world.

After bowling Australia out for 198 in the first innings, the visitors always looked the more likely to win.

They kept the pressure on throughout Sunday and didn’t panic when Cameron Green (104) brought up his third Test century after lunch on day four.

Green was offered no real support from his teammates and the Bangladeshis kept taking vital scalps to leave Australia on the ropes, with Mehidy Hasan Miraz taking 5-66.

The visitors went into the match with most observers giving them no chance of winning.

Their only warm-up game, against a Cricket Australia XI, ended in a big loss that included a second-innings collapse where they were all out for 54.

But they have completely outplayed the Australians and won every session, batting, bowling and catching better than their more illustrious counterparts.

Australia, fielding their best possible team, have looked out of sorts from the beginning.

Their batting failed in the first innings when they were bowled out on the opening day, then their much-vaunted bowling attack struggled against the gritty Bangladesh batsmen.

Led by a maiden Test century from opener Tanzid Hasan, Bangladesh made 426 and importantly kept Australia in the field for 138 overs in Darwin’s heat and humidity.

The bowlers then showed great patience Saturday to make regular breakthroughs and keep Australia under the cosh.

When Australia resumed Sunday on 161-4, most of their hopes lay with Alex Carey and Green.

Carey lived dangerously in the opening 30 minutes, twice edging seamer Hasan Mahmud through the vacant slips cordon for boundaries.

But on 30 Mehidy produced a beautiful ball, pitching in line then turning sharply to take Carey’s outside edge to wicketkeeper Litton Das.

He struck again soon after, bowling Webster for five to leave Australia 193-6 and in deep trouble.

A famous victory edged ever closer when Australia captain Pat Cummins pushed forward to a Mehidy delivery and got an inside edge to short leg, where Shadman Islam took a sharp chance.

Australia were 207-7, still 21 runs behind Bangladesh’s first-innings total.

Green and Mitchell Starc batted sensibly to ensure Bangladesh had to bat again.

Starc fell for 18 caught behind but Green was playing well and brought up his century shortly after lunch.

But despite looking increasingly comfortable, he was undone when a Hasan ball kept low, hit the toe end of his bat and cannoned into the stumps.

Mehidy wrapped up the innings when he trapped Nathan Lyon plumb in front leg before.

Depsite losing Tanzid in the first over, Mominul and Shadman Islam cruised to victory.

The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all six latest fatalities as suspected measles deaths.
With this, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 809, while confirmed deaths from measles have remained the same at 99.
A total of 1021 new suspected measles cases were reported during the 24-hour period, bringing the cumulative number of suspected cases nationwide to 142,797.
Meanwhile, 80 new confirmed measles cases were recorded, bringing the total number of laboratory-confirmed infections to 17,880.
Since March 15 this year, a total of 124,457 patients with suspected measles have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 119,939 have recovered, according to DGHS data.

item.title: Energy crisis will take 2 years to resolve: Finance Minister
item.description:
The ongoing energy crisis will take at least two years to resolve, Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury has said.

He said the problems surrounding gas and electricity could not be resolved within six months or a year and would require at least two years.

Explaining the timeframe, the finance minister said it would take around one and a half to two years to build a floating LNG terminal, meaning the crisis could not be resolved before then.

He made the remarks as the chief guest at an event organised by the American Chamber of Commerce in Bangladesh (AmCham) at Hotel InterContinental on Sunday afternoon.

The seminar focused on restoring investor confidence through policy reforms and effective implementation.

AmCham President Syed Mohammad Kamal chaired the event, where business leaders raised various concerns.

In his address, Amir Khasru said, “The economy cannot move forward without gas and electricity. However, we are swiftly taking whatever measures are possible. Gas exploration was neglected for a long time; now it is being resumed. Work is also under way on solar power and coal. We are determining how much of each type of energy will be required. The energy policy will be published within the next few weeks. People will then know what needs to be done. We will have to remain cautious over the next two years.”

Speaking on the government’s plans to increase revenue collection, the finance minister said the implementation and policy functions would be separated. The government was seeking to broaden the tax base, while a fixed-rate taxation system was being developed for small businesses alongside the creation of a database.

On the stock market, Amir Khasru said the government had been receiving warning signals and had subsequently introduced changes. “We need more listed companies,” he said.

Regarding the banking sector, the finance and planning minister said it was facing a severe capital shortfall that was too large for the government to cover. With the volume of non-performing loans also remaining high, he said alternative sources of financing were therefore needed.

The minister responded to various questions from business leaders at the meeting.

In his concluding remarks, AmCham President Syed Mohammad Kamal said, “We do not merely want to identify the challenges; we want to be part of the solution. This event has therefore been organised to rebuild confidence among businesses. More such initiatives will be held in the future.”

Two weeks after Hamas endorsed the latest stage of Trump's Gaza plan by saying it would hand over weapons to a new governing committee, Kushner pressed for verifiable disarmament, a key demand of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

item.title: Trump's envoys meet mediators, Israel strikes Gaza
item.description:
By Nidal al-Mughrabi

CAIRO, Aug 16 (Reuters) - Donald Trump's envoys met with Egyptian, Qatari and Turkish mediators in Cairo on Sunday, a diplomatic source said, in a bid to advance the U.S. president's Gaza peace plan, even as Israel pressed on with airstrikes in the enclave.

Hamas officials were present at some of the meetings between mediators and with Trump's envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and Nickolay Mladenov, Trump's Board of Peace envoy for Gaza, the diplomat said.
